#5237. What Is x402? How AI Agents Pay With Crypto

What Is x402? How AI Agents Pay With Crypto

Nobody really built the web with payments in mind. Early HTTP specifications included a status code, 402 "Payment Required", that was reserved for a future system of online payments. Then it sat unused for about 30 years. Payments were slow and expensive, and they needed accounts, card details and middlemen who could reverse charges. None of that works for a small payment made by software.

That gap matters more now because AI agents are starting to browse, call APIs and buy services for their users. An agent can't fill in a checkout form or sign up for a monthly plan for every tool it uses. Cloudflare says more than half of internet traffic is now non-human, and it reports seeing a billion HTTP 402 responses on its network every day.

x402 is an attempt to finally give the internet a native way to pay. This guide covers what it is, how it works, who backs it, and whether there's a token involved.

The 402 "Payment Required" code has been in the HTTP standard since the 1990s. It was set aside "for future use", and x402 is the first big effort to actually use it.

x402 is an open payment standard built on top of HTTP, the protocol that moves data around the web. Coinbase launched it in May 2025 with partners including AWS, Anthropic, Circle and NEAR. It lets APIs, apps and AI agents pay for services in stablecoins as part of an ordinary web request.

x402 is not a blockchain and it is not a coin. It's a set of rules: message formats, headers and a request-and-response flow that any server or client can follow. Payments are mostly made in USDC, Circle's dollar-backed stablecoin, with Coinbase's Ethereum layer-2 network Base as the main settlement chain. The protocol works with any chain, though, and it now supports Solana, Polygon, Arbitrum and others, as well as traditional card payments.

On April 2, 2026, the Linux Foundation announced it was launching the x402 Foundation, with Coinbase contributing the protocol and companies including Microsoft, Google, Visa and Mastercard expressing initial support. The new x402 Foundation became fully operational on July 14, 2026, and now stewards the protocol under vendor-neutral governance.

We are excited to introduce x402–a new open source payments protocol built on HTTP rails.

Let’s break it down: pic.twitter.com/9PNI49NK7A

— Coinbase Developer Platform🛡️ (@CoinbaseDev) May 6, 2025

x402 works through a short handshake inside a normal web request:

Most of the onchain work is done by a facilitator, a service that verifies payments and settles them on the blockchain so sellers don't have to run their own crypto setup. On EVM chains, x402 uses EIP-3009, a standard that lets someone transfer tokens by signing a permission instead of sending a transaction themselves. This means the buyer doesn't need to hold ETH for gas.

x402's main pitch is very small payments made by machines. Settlement on Base takes seconds and costs well under a cent, so it makes sense to pay fractions of a cent for a single API call. There's no sign-up, no API key and no subscription. The agent just pays and gets what it asked for.

Adoption has grown quickly. Coinbase released x402 V2 in December 2025, which added wallet-based identity so agents don't have to pay again on every call, automatic service discovery and support for more chains. In May 2026 it added batch settlement, where agents hand sellers signed vouchers that can be settled in bulk. x402 had processed more than 196 million transactions across 12 chains as of November 1, 2026, settling more than $42 million in total, according to Fireblocks, which cited data from tracker agenteconomy.to. Coinbase says more than 97% of onchain agent transactions in Q2 2026 used x402.

It's worth noting, however, that more than half of x402's lifetime transactions came from a two-month frenzy in late 2025, when traders ran automated scripts to mint and sell PING, a token issued through x402, according to Fireblocks. Activity has since settled at a much lower level: in October 2026, x402 processed 5.1 million transactions worth about $274,000.

No. x402 is a protocol, not a cryptocurrency, and it has no official native token. Payments are made in existing stablecoins, mostly USDC. Speculative "x402" tokens have appeared on various chains, but none of them is issued or backed by Coinbase or the x402 Foundation. Be very wary of any token that claims to be the official x402 coin.

To use x402, an agent or app needs a wallet holding a supported stablecoin on a supported network, usually USDC on Base. USDC is widely available on major exchanges including Coinbase, Kraken and Binance. Coinbase lets users send USDC straight to Base. Developers can also use Coinbase Developer Platform wallets or Circle Wallets to give their agents funds, and set spending limits to keep those agents under control.

The x402 Foundation is growing fast. It had 40 member organizations when it became operational in July 2026, and its member list has since grown to 57, including Visa, Mastercard, American Express, PayPal, Google, Shopify, Circle, Stripe and AWS. Michael Hursta became the foundation's executive director on October 1, 2026.

x402 isn't the only option, though. The Agentic Commerce Protocol, an open standard developed by Stripe and OpenAI, and Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol are competing for a role in agent payments, even though Stripe and Visa are also premier members of the x402 Foundation.

Stripe has also co-developed the Machine Payments Protocol with payments blockchain Tempo. Like x402, MPP uses the HTTP 402 code to let agents pay for services, but adds session-based billing so agents can pay as they go rather than settling every request onchain.

Since June 2026, it has also supported x402 payments. The big open question is whether x402's huge transaction counts turn into steady, real commerce. If they do, the payment code that sat unused for 30 years could end up carrying much of the AI economy's payments.

Bitcoin price fell from above $80,800 to near $76,600 on Thursday morning as a Nasdaq selloff in chip and AI stocks spilled into crypto.

Bitcoin price fell about 5% on Thursday morning, sliding from above $80,800 to near $76,000 as a sharp selloff in technology stocks spread into crypto and wiped out leveraged traders betting on further gains, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows.

The drop erased the rebound that had carried bitcoin back above $80,000 overnight. It touched a low near $76,100 shortly after the U.S. stock market opened, its weakest level since the start of the week.

The reversal came fast. Bitcoin held near $80,000 through Wednesday, and early Thursday traders were cheering a short squeeze that pushed it past $80,500. Within roughly two hours of the opening bell, the bitcoin price was more than $4,000 lower.

The trigger sat on Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled as much as 3.9% on Thursday and slipped into correction territory, trading 10% below the record close it set last month, CNBC reported. The S&P 500 fell about 2%, erasing Wednesday’s rally, its best session in three months.

Chip and AI stocks took the worst of it. Nvidia and Broadcom each fell about 5%, Tesla lost around 9% and neocloud names CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN dropped between 9% and 13%. Qualcomm slid 9% after a weak outlook. Sandisk was down nearly 19% at the time of writing.

Investors are pricing in a Democratic-controlled Congress after Tuesday’s midterms. Traders fear new limits on the data center buildout, and UBS analysts estimated that around 30% of U.S. data center capacity additions expected in 2028 could be at risk from construction pauses, Reuters reported. The selling started in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi closed down more than 5% as Samsung and SK hynix sank.

U.S. stocks shed $2.3 trillion in market value within the first hour of trading, with the Russell 2000 plunging 2.5% and on pace for its biggest one-day drop since June 5

Bitcoin price has traded alongside that AI-heavy tech complex for most of the year, and bitcoin miners are now part of it. Many have sold bitcoin to fund AI data centers, so the same political risk now weighs on both.

Leverage turned the move into a flush. Roughly $370 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated in about an hour as bitcoin broke $77,000 and ether fell below $2,300, most of them long bets. Wider tallies circulating on X put long liquidations closer to $400 million over the same 60 minutes.

The U.S. stock market shed more than $1 trillion in value within minutes of the open, and crypto went with it.

Wednesday’s short squeeze had pulled in late buyers with borrowed money. When stocks broke, those positions were the first to go, and forced selling pushed the bitcoin price through support around $77,000.

The macro backdrop offered little cover. Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 last week, matching July’s level, which was the lowest since 1969, Reuters reported. Economists had expected 196,000.

A labor market that tight gives the Federal Reserve little reason to ease. That leaves risk assets leaning on growth stories like AI to carry them, and that story is now under political pressure.

Fund flows were only a small offset. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs took in a net $74.6 million on Wednesday, breaking a three-day run of outflows, led by Fidelity’s FBTC while BlackRock’s IBIT saw money leave.

The next test is Friday’s October jobs report, followed by October CPI on Nov. 10 and the Fed’s Dec. 9 decision. Policy risk is building too, with House Democrats drafting their own market structure bill ahead of taking over the committees in January.

Traders are watching whether bitcoin can hold the $75,000 area, which held as support on election night and several times since August. A break would leave the bitcoin price near its lowest levels in months.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $76,200.

#5232. Canton Coin Gets SEC Nod as Wall Street Tokenization Heats Up

Canton Coin Gets SEC Nod as Wall Street Tokenization Heats Up

The blockchain behind Wall Street’s newest tokenization service just got a regulatory nod for its native token.

The SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance said in a letter dated Tuesday that it views Canton Coin, the native token of the Canton Network, as a “digital commodity” under the agency’s March interpretation of how securities laws apply to crypto.

Agency staff also said they won’t recommend enforcement action if Canton’s validators and application providers mint the token programmatically without registering it.

The relief comes a week after the Depository Trust & Clearing Corp. launched a tokenization service that runs on Canton and DTCC’s own private network, letting firms convert DTC-held stocks and Treasuries into tokens. Morgan Stanley said Tuesday that it was among the first banks to use the service.

SEC staff pointed to two representations from Canton’s lawyers. The first is that the token derives its value from the network’s programmatic operation and from supply and demand, rather than from the managerial efforts of others.

The second is that the network has no “central party.” Canton Coin launched without an initial coin offering or premine, and tokens were initially earned only by running network infrastructure and applications, according to a statement from Canton. Canton’s request letter was dated Oct. 30, four days before staff responded.

The letter has limits, though, as it reflects only staff’s position on enforcement, not a legal conclusion, and rests on the facts Canton presented, the SEC noted.

“Financial institutions need confidence in both the technology they use and the economic model that supports it,” said Yuval Rooz, CEO of Digital Asset, which created the Canton Network.

Canton said the letter is the first relief of its kind since the SEC published its March interpretive release, which found that most crypto assets aren’t securities. It’s also the first since the agency’s August Regulation Crypto Assets proposal.

The decision fits a broader shift since the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate in September, with the SEC and CFTC taking the lead on crypto rules. SEC Chair Paul Atkins said in July the agency was ready to act if Congress didn’t, and the SEC recently proposed rules on how advisers and funds hold crypto.

Digital Asset raised $355 million earlier this year from Wall Street firms and a sovereign wealth fund.

#5230. XRP sellers face massive slip as USD order book depth fakes size

At the Nov. 4 close, a capped sample of Bitstamp-issued USD offers held less funded inventory than the smaller RLUSD book.

An XRP Ledger order book sample advertised 1.28 million Bitstamp-issued USD tokens at the Nov. 4 close, but the offer owners' balances funded only about 57,000.

For an XRP holder selling into those offers, the headline quantity overstated the token inventory available to trade.

The smaller sample for dollar stablecoin Ripple USD (RLUSD) held about 92,000 funded tokens, with no gap between quoted and funded amounts at that ledger.

A Nov. 5 refresh, at ledger 108132129, closed at 13:09 UTC, still showed a large Bitstamp-dollar gap of roughly 1.31 million tokens quoted against 58,179 funded. RLUSD had about 80,435 quoted and 75,726 funded, so its earlier fully funded reading had not persisted.

The Nov. 4 reading covered validated ledger 108120236, closed at 23:59:51 UTC. Bitstamp-issued USD offers totaled 1,280,737 tokens quoted and 56,887 funded, a funded share of 4.44%.

One offer advertised 1,241,760 USD tokens while its funded amount was only 17,967. That single offer accounted for almost the entire difference, showing why adding advertised order sizes can mislead about what a counterparty can deliver.

The measurement requests at most 100 offers per side and counts quantities within 10% of each book's own reference midpoint, derived from its tightest uncrossed bid and ask. NOSHASHI, the ledger-data service, calls the dollar-token side that XRP sellers receive the “ask.”

XRPL's offer rules allow an owner to advertise more than it currently holds because placing an offer does not lock its full amount. The official book offers interface normally omits unfunded offers and identifies partially funded amounts, so software can distinguish advertised size from supported size.

An oversized Bitstamp USD offer drove the November 4 gap. Compare both book samples at the next day's measured ledger.

At the November 4 close, the smaller RLUSD sample had more funded inventory than the much larger quoted Bitstamp-dollar sample.

At the refreshed November 5 ledger, RLUSD was partly funded too, but its sampled funded inventory still exceeded Bitstamp USD.

A larger advertised book can contain less funded token inventory for XRP sellers.

#5228. U.S.-Sanctioned Moscow Exchange Will List Bitcoin on Dec. 1 as Russia Pulls Crypto Trading Home

Russia's largest exchange, Moscow Exchange,. will open bitcoin trading on Dec. 1 under the country's new crypto law, with retail buyers tested and capped at 300,000 rubles a year.

Moscow Exchange, Russia’s largest trading venue, will begin trading bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT on Dec. 1, the exchange announced this week, calling it the country’s first organized market for digital currencies.

The launch puts bitcoin on the same screens Russians use to trade Sberbank and Gazprom shares. It also puts a major crypto venue inside an institution that sits under U.S. sanctions. The first phase will run as a pilot. Participants will connect as they are ready, and the exchange said interest has come from existing members, their clients and businesses that already use digital currencies for investment and settlement.

Trading will run on the exchange’s existing stock market technology and follow its stock market hours, from 6:50 a.m. to 11:50 p.m. Moscow time, the exchange told Russian newspaper Vedomosti. The National Clearing Centre, the exchange’s clearing arm, will clear every trade.

From day one, clients can settle trades the same day or the next day, and the exchange will offer swaps to help participants manage liquidity. BTC, ETH and USDT will trade in both addressed and addressless modes, and the list is set to grow over time with Russian and international instruments.

Custody will run through partner digital depositaries, a new type of entity created under the country’s rules. A Moscow Exchange executive first previewed the plan on Oct. 31.

Retail access is tight. Non-qualified investors must pass a test before they can buy, and they can purchase no more than 300,000 rubles of digital currency a year, roughly $3,700, through a single broker. Qualified investors face no cap. The exchange had first flagged plans to debut bitcoin trading in October.

For the exchange, the structure keeps crypto inside a regime it already runs. Brokers connect the way they do for equities, trades net through the same clearing system and investor classifications carry over from the stock market. That lowers the barrier for banks and brokerages that want to offer bitcoin without building separate custody and matching systems of their own.

The U.S. Treasury blocked Moscow Exchange and the National Clearing Centre in June 2024 as part of a broader push against Russia’s financial system over the war in Ukraine. That makes the clearing house holding customers’ USDT a sanctioned entity.

Tether routinely freezes wallets tied to addresses on the Treasury’s sanctions list, which raises questions about how the stablecoin issuer would treat USDT held through the Moscow clearing structure. Neither the exchange nor Tether has publicly addressed that issue.

The choice of USDT, a dollar-pegged token, is notable for a market built in part to operate outside the dollar system. Bitcoin and ether carry no issuer that can freeze balances.

The market rests on Federal Law No. 282-FZ, “On Digital Currencies and Digital Rights,” whose main provisions took effect on Sept. 1. The law still bans using crypto for domestic payments, though exporters and importers can use it to settle cross-border trade.

Russian officials have spent the past year building the plumbing. Lawmakers handed securities regulators oversight of crypto last month, and the central bank licensed Sberbank for crypto work weeks earlier.

The goal is to move trading that Russians already do on offshore exchanges and peer-to-peer desks onto domestic, supervised rails where the state can see it and tax it. Moscow is betting that a familiar exchange, tied to brokers that Russian investors already use, can pull that volume back.

The open question is whether the caps and testing keep retail traders offshore, and whether foreign liquidity will touch a sanctioned venue at all. For now, Russia’s first organized bitcoin market opens on Dec. 1, with a pilot and a modest ceiling.

#5226. US Voters Back AI Data Center Restrictions in At Least 29 Communities

US Voters Back AI Data Center Restrictions in At Least 29 Communities

Voters in at least 29 U.S. jurisdictions backed bans or restrictions on data-center development Tuesday, according to The Washington Post, dealing a new setback to the massive infrastructure buildout behind artificial intelligence.

The measures ranged from outright prohibitions to requirements for additional public approval. Some were nonbinding advisory votes, meaning their passage does not automatically stop construction.

Ballotpedia tracked 41 data-center measures on November 3 ballots across 10 states. Twenty-eight were framed so that a yes vote would curb development, while 13 would permit or support projects, meaning rejecting one of the latter could also count as a defeat for developers.

Ohio produced some of the clearest results. All 10 charter measures backed by the grassroots group Conserve Ohio passed, according to the Post, and more than three-quarters of voters in Hubbard, Ohio, supported a ban on data centers.

The negative sentiment is so big that voters in Granville, Trenton, and Sunbury backed restrictions with margins of roughly 78% to 82%.

In Illinois, nearly 80% of voters in Joliet Township rejected an advisory proposal supporting AI data centers. In Janesville, Wisconsin, more than 60% approved a requirement for another public vote before major development at a former General Motors site linked to a proposed data center.

These facilities house the chips and servers used to train and run AI systems. Their appetite for electricity has turned proposed campuses into local fights over utility bills and grid capacity, while opponents also raise concerns about water use, noise and deals struck without public scrutiny.

AI companies are aware of the growing backlash and are already working to counter it. Some are stepping up lobbying efforts, while others are turning to public relations campaigns to reshape public perception. OpenAI, for instance, has sought to rebrand data centers as “compute campuses,” in an effort to distance the facilities from the negative connotations increasingly associated with them.

The votes arrived alongside victories by politicians promising tougher oversight of data centers. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas after campaigning for a moratorium on new projects, while Ohio's governor-elect Amy Acton also supports a pause and stricter rules.

Industry leaders have warned that blanket restrictions would put U.S. AI investment at risk. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said last month that a broad moratorium could have serious economic consequences. "If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession," he said.

#5224. FBI agent drains crypto wallets tied to 35 investigations, steals $2.47 million and plans Portugal escape

The former counterintelligence agent used sensitive wallet credentials to execute roughly 100 fraudulent transfers.

A former FBI agent stole $2.47 million in crypto using classified investigative records, compromising federal investigations into criminal organizations and foreign adversaries.

The US Department of Justice disclosed on Nov. 5 that Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after exploiting his access to crypto wallet credentials collected during FBI investigations.

His scheme involved about 100 unauthorized transfers using credentials tied to 35 separate FBI investigations, including wallets belonging to suspected criminals, adversarial nation-state actors, and at least one wallet the bureau created for an operation.

Prosecutors said the thefts compromised multiple investigations involving criminal groups and foreign adversaries, along with sensitive intelligence-gathering methods.

The disclosure exposes a significant internal security failure at the FBI, where an agent entrusted with protecting national security turned information gathered through federal investigations into personal enrichment.

According to prosecutors, Yaroch worked in the FBI's Boston Division from 2017 until early 2025, investigating threats involving a foreign adversary.

He subsequently joined the bureau's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, where he had access to systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained through investigations.

The thefts began no later than December 2024, before his transfer to the division.

An FBI affidavit filed in August revealed that Yaroch searched bureau records for crypto wallets associated with foreign adversaries, memorized their recovery credentials, and transferred funds into a personal wallet.

Two routes intersected: access to wallet secrets in FBI records enabled transfers from investigation-linked wallets.

Investigative access to wallet credentials enabled personal transfers, including from at least one FBI operational wallet.

However, the misconduct expanded into a broader theft and money laundering scheme.

After taking the crypto, Yaroch converted portions into other digital assets and moved funds through additional transactions to conceal their origins.

Between November 2025 and January 2026, he transferred approximately $93,082 into an account and used money moved between his accounts to cover credit card bills, vehicle payments, and other debts.

The Justice Department said his actions interfered with the FBI's ability to protect public safety and national security while compromising sources and methods used in criminal investigations and foreign intelligence collection.

Prosecutors did not identify the affected countries or investigations, leaving the full extent of the intelligence damage undisclosed.

Beyond paying personal debts, Yaroch was preparing to use the proceeds to establish a new life in Europe, according to federal investigators.

Court documents revealed that the former agent turned to ChatGPT for advice on investing approximately $1 million and relocating to the European Union.

After discussing his interest in vineyard ownership and a slower lifestyle, the AI chatbot recommended Portugal as a potential destination.

Yaroch subsequently took concrete steps toward establishing himself in the country.

On June 15, he granted power of attorney to Portuguese lawyers to register him with the country's tax authorities and obtain a tax identification number.

Investigators also discovered plans for a September trip to Portugal. The August affidavit disclosed that Yaroch had previously traveled abroad without reporting some of those trips to the FBI, despite security requirements.

His plans unraveled in July when he voluntarily disclosed his cryptocurrency thefts to Justice Department personnel.

The initial investigation identified roughly $1 million in suspected stolen cryptocurrency. However, the subsequent criminal case found that the scheme generated about $2.47 million.

The FBI terminated his employment on July 31, and investigators recovered approximately $925,426 in cryptocurrency from accounts he controlled that day. An additional $165,582 remained in dollars at Kraken, according to the affidavit.

Yaroch is scheduled to be sentenced on March 4, 2027, and faces up to 20 years in prison.

#5222. US Bank Regulator Issues First AI Framework as Banks Battle Rogue Agents

US Bank Regulator Issues First AI Framework as Banks Battle Rogue Agents

The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued its first supervisory framework for artificial intelligence in banking today, telling examiners to focus less on how powerful an AI system is and more on what happens when it makes a mistake.

The OCC's framework addresses that very concern, although the regulator has not linked its issuance to those specific incidents.

In a section covering operational resilience, the agency warns that external agents operated by customers, fintechs, or other businesses could create risks for banks even when the banks don't control those systems.

It suggests examiners consider measures including identity verification, delegated permissions, transaction limits, monitoring, and the ability to suspend or revoke access.

The guidelines aim to tackle the dilemma of how to let customers use AI assistants to manage their finances without giving autonomous software unrestricted access to accounts that banks are already facing.

The new OCC guidance arrives less than two weeks after reports that major banks were discovering unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, sometimes taking actions that appeared to go beyond users' instructions.

Morgan Stanley was blocking outside agents, while JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi were restricting access, according to an Axios report on October 22. Bank executives described the situation as "horrifying," raising questions about who controls an autonomous agent once it has access to someone's money.

The OCC's framework makes a distinction between an AI system's technical sophistication and the damage it could cause.

A simple agent authorized to initiate financial transactions may present greater risk than a more advanced model limited to writing internal documents, the regulator said.

Under the 22-page framework, examiners can consider the consequences of failure, whether an action can be reversed, and how much control humans retain over the system.

The agency outlines four illustrative risk tiers. Fully autonomous payment agents and real-time credit decision systems fall into the highest category, while basic internal productivity tools occupy the lowest.

Higher-risk systems may warrant tighter restrictions on autonomy, independent testing, and human approval before consequential actions can proceed.

The framework also addresses AI systems that continue operating while making harmful decisions. Suggested safeguards include circuit breakers, rate limits, restricted permissions, and emergency shutdown controls.

Those considerations are especially relevant to the outside agents described in Axios's earlier reporting, where banks struggled to distinguish legitimate customer-authorized software from systems operating beyond their intended permissions.

The OCC stressed that the document does not create new regulatory requirements or enforceable standards for banks.

Instead, it gives examiners a way to evaluate AI within existing operational, compliance, and cybersecurity risk categories. Banks are not required to establish a separate AI risk category.

The document uses the mandatory term "Super Intelligence," which the Donald Trump administration insists on using in place of “artificial intelligence,” but its scope includes conventional AI and “autonomous agents” rather than only hypothetical systems with intelligence beyond human capabilities.

The framework covers AI used in payments, fraud detection, customer service, and other banking operations. It also extends its risk considerations to external AI agents connecting through bank channels.

The OCC said it intends to update the guidance as the technology develops. For now, its illustrative risk scale puts autonomous payment agents in the highest-risk category, regardless of how well they perform in testing.

#5221. Keel (KEEL) Sells Entire Bitcoin Treasury for $192 Million, Will Sell BTC Daily

Keel sold 2,520 bitcoin in the third quarter, left its treasury near zero and said Quebec-mined coins will now be sold every day as it pivots to AI data centers.

Keel Infrastructure sold its entire bitcoin treasury in the third quarter, offloading 2,520 bitcoin for $192 million and leaving the company with only nominal holdings at Sept. 30, the former Bitfarms miner reported Thursday.

The sales covered the 2,261 bitcoin Keel held going into the quarter plus the 259 it mined, and the company said it timed them during periods of strength. Going forward, bitcoin mined from Keel’s remaining Quebec operations will be sold on a daily basis, “effectively eliminating the Company’s exposure to Bitcoin price movements on treasury holdings.”

The move completes a shift Keel began earlier this year, when the company, then still trading as Bitfarms (BITF), started selling its stack and winding down U.S. mining to fund high-performance computing and AI infrastructure.

Keel Infrastructure Corp. rebranded from Bitfarms after completing a U.S. redomiciliation to Delaware in April and now describes itself as a North American digital infrastructure and energy company. Legacy bitcoin mining still shows up in the results, but the center of gravity has moved.

Revenue from continuing operations fell to $28 million from $68 million a year earlier, largely because Keel stopped U.S. bitcoin mining in the second quarter and because the average bitcoin price declined. Adjusted EBITDA swung to a negative $27 million from a positive $19 million. General and administrative expenses roughly doubled to $34 million as the company hired senior specialists and booked higher stock-based compensation. The company still posted about $780 million of unrestricted cash as of Nov. 4 and said it has no current need for debt or equity financing before signing a lease.

“Power supply is getting scarcer while demand keeps climbing,” CEO Ben Gagnon said in the release. “Keel’s 2027 and 2028 power is further advanced, more secure, and closer to delivery than it was last quarter.”

CFO Jonathan Mir added that capital deployed ahead of a lease becomes equity in project financing and that the company examines opportunities to recycle capital on an ongoing basis.

Construction began at Moses Lake in September after Keel cleared Notice to Proceed, and the company expects it to be the first energized site generating HPC revenue in 2027. It also engineered an optional plan for next-generation Vera Rubin architecture at the site. Permitting advanced at Sharon and Panther Creek in Pennsylvania, and load studies could expand secured data center capacity from 478 MW toward nearly 1.9 GW if Panther Creek and Scrubgrass expansions proceed. Keel has also moved to consolidate older bitcoin sites into a single AI campus.

The development pipeline stands at about 2.2 gigawatts with grid interconnections already in place across Pennsylvania, Washington State and Québec. That is the inventory Keel is trying to lease before the cash from the bitcoin sale and the remaining Quebec mining runs down.

Keel is not alone. Riot Platforms and Hut 8 have sold thousands of bitcoin this year to fund AI builds and share buybacks, and Riot this week named Anthropic as the tenant on a roughly $28 billion Texas lease. Public miners that once marketed themselves as bitcoin accumulators are turning their power and land into AI capacity instead.

Keel’s remaining mining footprint sits in Quebec, where regulated power rates still support production. Those coins will no longer sit on the balance sheet. The company will sell them the day they are mined, converting hashrate into cash for the infrastructure build rather than into a treasury that moves with the bitcoin price.

The open question is whether the leases close on the terms Gagnon described before the cash pile is spent. Keel says competitive tension is high at all three near-term sites and that multiple creditworthy parties are at the table. Until a signed lease shows up, the $192 million bitcoin sale is the clearest proof that the company has left the treasury strategy behind.

#5220. NYSE-backed crypto venture faces 90% stock rejection as $92 liquidity problem threatens tokenization dream

Apple, Nvidia and 65 other companies have objected to OKXICE's plans, while thin liquidity across existing tokenized stock markets raises a second major obstacle to its launch.

More than 90% of the stocks targeted by OKX and NYSE-backed tokenization venture now face objections from their issuers.

A comparison of OKXICE's latest regulatory notice with its original October proposal shows that companies have objected to 57 of the 63 stock tickers initially earmarked for trading.

The objections, which have grown to 67 companies overall, include Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Tesla, and Meta, threatening to strip the proposed blockchain-based marketplace of many of Wall Street's most widely traded names before its launch.

The setback comes just weeks after the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) introduced a regulatory exemption designed to accelerate tokenized stock trading, allowing qualifying platforms to offer blockchain-based shares through automated trading pools.

OKXICE, a joint venture equally owned by crypto exchange OKX's US holding company and Intercontinental Exchange, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange, plans to let investors trade tokenized versions of US stocks around the clock using stablecoins.

However, the growing corporate resistance has left the venture facing questions about which securities it can offer and whether investors will have sufficient liquidity to trade them.

The scale of the resistance has grown rapidly since OKXICE outlined its plans in early October.

By Oct. 30, 50 companies had registered objections. That figure rose to 62 by Nov. 4 before another five companies, including Meta, Palantir, S&P Global, KLA and Super Micro Computer, joined the list on Nov. 5.

Of the original 62 companies identified by OKXICE, 56 have now objected. The original proposal covered 63 tickers because Alphabet's two share classes were listed separately.

That leaves just six companies from the initial lineup without disclosed objections: Strategy, Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Securitize and BitGo.

All six have substantial connections to the cryptocurrency or digital asset industry, highlighting how far the venture's potential stock selection has shifted from the broader US equity market.

However, the absence of an objection does not establish that those companies have endorsed the proposal or that their tokenized shares will be available when trading begins.

The resistance is particularly significant because of how the SEC structured its September exemption.

Under the framework, companies whose shares are tokenized by unaffiliated third parties must receive written notice and an opportunity to object. A formal objection prevents the venue from offering those third-party tokenized shares under the exemption.

The framework leaves room for issuer-backed tokenization, meaning the objections do not necessarily represent opposition to blockchain-based securities in general.

Nevertheless, OKXICE has yet to announce a launch date or confirm how many stocks will ultimately be available. Its public website continues to advertise the trading venue as forthcoming.

Even if OKXICE secures a viable selection of stocks, it faces another challenge: attracting enough capital to support trading.

The tokenization venture disclosed that neither it nor its affiliates will provide liquidity to its proposed marketplace.

Instead, eligible outside participants, including market makers and institutional investors, would need to deposit stock tokens and stablecoins into trading pools that facilitate transactions.

That model places considerable importance on the willingness of independent investors to commit capital, particularly outside traditional US market hours.

Existing tokenized equity markets offer a warning about the difficulties involved.

According to Dune's After Issuance report, the median decentralized trading pool for tokenized equities held just $92 as of Aug. 31.

Across 5,484 pools containing $69 million in assets, just 78 pools accounted for approximately $56 million, or 81% of the measured holdings. By protocol, Dune located $34 million on Uniswap, $17 million on PancakeSwap, and $11 million on Raydium.

This shows how concentrated liquidity remains across decentralized equity markets, despite growing interest in bringing traditional securities on-chain.

The $92 figure represents the median holdings of existing pools, rather than the liquidity available for every stock or a forecast of trading conditions on OKXICE.

The venture plans to use Uniswap v4-based pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain, where tokenized shares will trade against stablecoins through approved wallets.

Unlike conventional stock exchanges that match buyers and sellers through order books, the proposed system relies on assets deposited into pools to execute trades.

Insufficient capital in those pools could cause significant price slippage, particularly when investors try to execute large transactions or sell positions during market volatility.

That creates a significant challenge for a venture promising access to US equities beyond Wall Street's regular trading hours.

OKXICE must now overcome substantial issuer resistance while convincing outside market participants to finance trading in whatever tokenized stocks remain available.

Its eventual launch will provide the first meaningful test of whether the venue can assemble enough eligible securities and trading capital to deliver on its round-the-clock ambitions.
